prompt: `OpenDemo` set `book.year = -1899` on a class with a public field. What happened?
hint: Read the one line it printed.

choices.text: The compiler refused the negative value
choices.why: The compiler checks types, and `-1899` is a perfectly good `int`.

choices.text: Nothing objected; it printed `-1899`
choices.why: Right: a public field has no code of its own that runs when it is written.

choices.text: The JVM threw an `IllegalArgumentException` when the field was written
choices.why: That exception came from `checkYear` in `Book`; `OpenBook` has no such check.

choices.text: The year was stored as 1899, its absolute value
choices.why: Java stores exactly the `int` it is given; nothing corrected it.

prompt: Why does `Book`'s constructor call `checkYear` too, and not only `setYear`?
hint: Think of `new Book("x", -1899)`.

choices.text: Because a constructor cannot call a setter
choices.why: It can; the lesson routes both through one private method so the rule exists once.

choices.text: To make the stack trace one line shorter when a bad year arrives through the constructor
choices.why: The stack trace is a side effect; the point is which writes are checked.

choices.text: Otherwise building a book would be a way round the rule
choices.why: Right: every write must pass the check, the first one included.

prompt: `Sneaky` wrote `book.year = -1899` on the private-field `Book`. What stopped it?
hint: The message started with the file name and a line number.

choices.text: The compiler, before anything ran
choices.why: Right: `year has private access in Book`, and there was nothing to run.

choices.text: `checkYear`, which threw when the field changed
choices.why: `checkYear` runs only when called; a direct write would skip it, which is why the compiler forbids one.

choices.text: The JVM's verifier, when it loaded `Sneaky.class`
choices.why: There was no `Sneaky.class`: `javac` reported an error and wrote nothing.

choices.text: The `final` on the field
choices.why: `year` is not final, since `setYear` changes it; `title` is the final one.

prompt: By the JavaBeans naming convention, the getter of a `boolean` field called `available` is named `___`.
hint: For a `boolean`, `is` replaces `get`.

prompt: A setter that only does `this.year = year;` checks nothing. What does it still buy over a public field?
hint: Think of the day a rule arrives.

choices.text: Faster access, because the JIT compiles the method
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; a field access is at least as fast.

choices.text: A single place for a future check
choices.why: Right: the rule goes into the setter and every caller gets it.

choices.text: Protection against a negative year, since setters reject negatives by default
choices.why: A setter does only what its body says; this one says nothing.

choices.text: Nothing at all; the two are identical in every respect
choices.why: They behave the same today, and differ the day the rule has to change.

prompt: Which of these choices in `Book` protect the rule that a year lies between 1450 and 2100? Choose all that apply.
hint: Find every way a year could get in.

choices.text: `year` is `private`
choices.why: Yes: no code outside `Book` can write it directly.

choices.text: The constructor passes its argument through `checkYear`
choices.why: Yes: the first write is checked like every other.

choices.text: `title` is `final`
choices.why: That fixes the title; it says nothing about the year.

choices.text: `setYear` passes its argument through `checkYear`
choices.why: Yes: changes after construction are checked too.

choices.text: `getYear` returns an `int` rather than an `Integer`
choices.why: Reading cannot break the rule; the type of the return changes nothing here.

prompt: `Shelf.titles` is `private final`, yet `LeakDemo` put three books on a shelf for two. How?
hint: What exactly did `getTitles()` return?

choices.text: `final` stops the list being replaced, so `add` on the shelf skipped its check
choices.why: `Shelf.add` was never called the third time; `ArrayList.add` was.

choices.text: The getter returned the shelf's own list, and the caller added a third book straight to it
choices.why: Right: `private` hides the name, not the object a reference leads to.

choices.text: A third `add` is allowed when the capacity is even
choices.why: There is no such rule; the check is `titles.size() == capacity`.

choices.text: `getTitles()` returned a copy, and the copy grew past the limit
choices.why: A copy growing would leave the shelf at two; the shelf itself reported three.

prompt: What does `final` on `private final List<String> titles` guarantee?
hint: A reference and the object it refers to are two things.

choices.text: That nobody can add to or remove from the list, from inside the class or from outside it
choices.why: The list stayed an ordinary `ArrayList`, and `LeakDemo` added to it.

choices.text: That the getter returns a copy
choices.why: `final` does nothing to what a method returns.

choices.text: That the field refers to the same list for the object's whole life
choices.why: Right: the reference is fixed; the list's contents are not.

prompt: In `SafeDemo`, `copy` and `view` were taken, and then `Iracema` was added to the shelf. Why did only `view` show it?
hint: One of them is a new list; the other is a window.

choices.text: `List.copyOf` made a new list at that moment; the view looks through to the shelf's own list
choices.why: Right: later changes reach the view and never the copy.

choices.text: `Collections.unmodifiableList` refreshes itself each time the shelf calls `add`
choices.why: Nothing is refreshed; the view has no copy of its own to refresh.

choices.text: `copy` was printed before `Iracema` was added
choices.why: Both were printed after the `add`; the order of the `println` lines does not explain it.

choices.text: Copies drop the last element added to the original
choices.why: The copy held everything there was when it was made: one title.

prompt: What did `view.add("O Guarani")` do?
hint: The last three lines of the transcript.

choices.text: Added the book, since the shelf's capacity was 3
choices.why: The view refuses every change, whatever the capacity.

choices.text: Threw `IllegalStateException: shelf is full`
choices.why: That message comes from `SafeShelf.add`, which this call never reached.

choices.text: Threw `UnsupportedOperationException`
choices.why: Right: a read-only view refuses `add`, on the line that tried.

prompt: Match each way of returning `titles` to what the caller can do with the result.
hint: The table in the section, plus the leaking `Shelf`.

pairs.right: Read a snapshot that never changes
Read the current list, and change nothing

right_distractors: Change the snapshot without touching the shelf

prompt: A constructor `Shelf(List<String> titles)` does `this.titles = titles;`. The getter returns a copy. How can a caller still break the capacity?
hint: Who else holds the list that was passed in?

choices.text: It cannot: copying on the way out closes every door
choices.why: The list came in from the caller, who still holds it.

choices.text: By calling the constructor twice on the same object
choices.why: A constructor runs once per object; that is not a way in.

choices.text: By adding to the list it passed in, which is now the shelf's field
choices.why: Right: copy what you receive, `new ArrayList<>(titles)`, as well as what you return.

choices.text: By reading the copy and casting it back to `ArrayList` to reach the shelf's own list
choices.why: A copy from `List.copyOf` is not the shelf's list, whatever it is cast to.

prompt: `AskDemo` printed the right fee. What is wrong with it?
hint: Where is the fee rule written?

choices.text: It uses `long` for money, which loses cents
choices.why: A `long` count of cents loses nothing; that is the safe choice.

choices.text: The rule lives in the caller, so every other caller must repeat it
choices.why: Right: the receipt, the e-mail and the account page would each copy the same lines.

choices.text: It charges a negative fee for a loan returned early
choices.why: The `late > 0` guard prevents that; the risk is the next caller forgetting it.

choices.text: `getDue()` exposes a mutable date
choices.why: `LocalDate` cannot be changed once built, so handing it out is safe.

prompt: What did `TellDemo` print for a loan due on 9 October, checked on 5 October?
hint: The second line of output.

choices.text: `Iracema: -200 cents`
choices.why: Four days early would be -200 without the guard, and `lateFeeCents` has it.

choices.text: `Iracema: 0 cents`
choices.why: Right: a loan that is not late yet owes nothing.

choices.text: `Iracema: 150 cents`
choices.why: That was the first line, for 12 October.

prompt: With `FEE_PER_DAY_CENTS = 50`, what does `lateFeeCents` return for a loan due on 9 October, checked on 19 October? Give cents.
hint: Days late times fifty.

prompt: Why does `describe` take `today` as a parameter instead of calling `LocalDate.now()` itself?
hint: Think of a test written on any day of the year.

choices.text: So that the same loan gives the same answer whatever day the code runs
choices.why: Right: the caller decides what today is, and a test can fix it.

choices.text: Because `LocalDate.now()` is not allowed inside a class with private fields
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; it was a choice about predictability.

choices.text: Because `LocalDate.now()` returns a mutable object
choices.why: `LocalDate` is immutable, whoever creates it.

prompt: A class carries a row read from a CSV file to the code that saves it, and decides nothing. Following the section, how should it be written?
hint: Some data is only data.

choices.text: With private fields, no getters, and methods for every rule
choices.why: It has no rules; inventing behaviour for it would be ceremony.

choices.text: With public mutable fields, since accessors are red tape and this class has no rule to protect
choices.why: Mutable public fields bring back every problem of section 02.

choices.text: As a record, whose accessors exist because reading the values is the point
choices.why: Right: lesson 29's `record` is the tool for data that is only data.

prompt: A `Member` class has `private final List<Loan> loans` and promises at most five loans. Which getter keeps that promise and still lets a screen show the member's current loans as they change?
hint: The screen must see later changes and make none.

choices.text: `return loans;`
choices.why: The screen could then add a sixth loan to the member's own list.

choices.text: `return List.copyOf(loans);`
choices.why: Safe, but frozen: the screen would not see loans added after it asked.

choices.text: `return Collections.unmodifiableList(loans);`
choices.why: Right: a read-only window that follows the member's list.

choices.text: `return new ArrayList<>(loans);`
choices.why: A fresh copy: changes to it are harmless, and it is just as frozen as `copyOf`.

prompt: Every caller of `loan.getDue()` compares it with today and charges a fee. What does the section suggest?
hint: Who should own the sum?

choices.text: Make `due` public, since every caller reads it anyway and a getter adds nothing to that
choices.why: That spreads the rule further and gives up the date's protection.

choices.text: Move the fee into a method on `Loan`, and drop the getter if nothing else reads it
choices.why: Right: tell the loan what you need, and the rule exists once.

choices.text: Add a setter for `due` so callers can correct it
choices.why: Nobody needs to change the date; they need the fee.
